title: 1911 Triangle Shirtwaist factory decision whether production/security controls may compromise emergency egress

decision_cutoff.date_or_period: Before the Triangle Shirtwaist factory fire of 25 March 1911
decision_cutoff.definition: The factory owners/managers' ongoing workplace-safety and access-control decision whether exit doors and other fire protections should be configured primarily for worker/theft control and low operating cost, or whether unobstructed emergency egress and stronger fire precautions should take priority.

packets.masking_note: Names Triangle Shirtwaist, New York and the high-rise garment-factory context.
Names/date/industry removed; preserves high-rise factory, low-power workforce, flammable material, exit-control and safety-cost structure.

expected_constitutional_constraints: An employer may protect property and manage attendance, but theft/control benefits do not justify transferring catastrophic emergency-egress risk onto workers.
Workers' economic dependence and limited bargaining power strengthen the employer's duty not to treat formal employment consent as consent to avoidable lethal hazards.

Where a low-cost less-dangerous alternative can achieve the legitimate security objective — e.g. unlocked emergency egress plus guards/checks or other controls — the more dangerous arrangement fails a least-harmful-means test.
Profit/productivity savings from foregoing reasonable fire precautions are extracted benefits if workers disproportionately bear the resulting injury/death risk.
The case evaluates system design and foreseeable risk rather than presuming individual criminal intent by particular owners.
Safety rules should be explicit, inspectable and enforceable rather than depending entirely on workers challenging their employer during ordinary production.
